http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/26/ice-a.text: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested nearly 50,000 people in July, the highest monthly total since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, according to new figures.ICE made 49,571 arrests in July, up 15% from 43,021 in June and 70% from 29,241 in February, according to government data analysed by the Associated Press news agency.The surge in immigration arrests comes as the Trump administration continues to pursue its mass deportation agenda, shifting from high-profile operations in major US cities to less visible enforcement actions.As arrests have surged in recent weeks, boosted by increased hiring, ICE has detained people during traffic stops and increasingly relied on state and local law enforcement agencies to carry out immigration enforcement duties.ICE officers have also begun arresting Haitians who have lost protections from deportation.The new arrest numbers show the administration “didn’t stop the enforcement,” said Mark Krikorian of the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for more immigration restrictions.“They changed the tactics and are, if anything, being more effective.”State partnerships become key to immigration enforcementThe number of arrests made by state and local police departments who partner with ICE has dramatically increased over the last year.Those partnerships, which ICE has grown with the help of generous financial incentives for participating agencies, accounted for 6,500 arrests in July, or about 13% of the total, the data showed. A year earlier, they accounted for less than 5% of ICE’s monthly arrests.Texas and Florida accounted for nearly 20,000 arrests in July, highlighting the growing role of the two states in the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda.Both states have expanded cooperation with ICE through so-called 287(g) agreements, which allow state and local law enforcement officers to carry out certain federal immigration enforcement duties.Over half of immigrants arrested had no criminal historyThe Trump administration has repeatedly said its immigration enforcement operations target people who have committed crimes in the US as part of efforts to improve public safety.However, the data shows that more than half of those arrested in July had no criminal convictions and were not facing criminal charges. Less than a quarter had been convicted of a crime.Half of the arrests were non-custodial, meaning ICE agents detained people in the community rather than taking custody of those already held in prisons or by local police.At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration agents since Trump returned to office and launched his immigration crackdown.

Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty Images US news Russia plotting to kill Ukraine allies in US and Europe, FBI says Intelligence services allegedly attempted to pay people to surveil and kill people perceived to be aligned with Ukraine Associated Press Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.28 EDT First published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia’s intelligence services are plotting to carry out targeted killings in the United States and in European nations supporting Ukraine , federal authorities said Tuesday as they announced charges against five people who remain at large. An indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court said a network of the intelligence services had paid and attempted to pay individuals in the United States and in other countries to surveil targets to be killed with plans to then kill them. The associates recruited in the network also had been solicited to carry out acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that were perceived to be aligned with Ukraine, the indictment said. James Barnacle Jr, head of New York’s FBI office, said the FBI disrupted the plans “through relentless work” as members of the Russian intelligence services and their affiliates “conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world”. Darren Cox, head of the Washington DC office of the FBI , cited “extraordinary work by multiple FBI field offices, components, and partner agencies that collectively disrupted Russia’s attempts to conduct violent acts in our nation’s capital and throughout the United States”. He said in a release that when the threat was first identified, the FBI’s Washington field office and its partners “moved quickly to disrupt the plot and hold the Russian government accountable for its actions”. According to the release, a network of people working for the Russian Federation’s intelligence services had since at least 2024 conspired to conduct and had conducted attacks and murders around the world, including within the United States. It called the Russian intelligence services network “one arm” of the Russian Federation’s apparatus designed to carry out external attacks, including murder, around the world. Previously, the release said, the network had focused on Russian dissidents and defectors but most recently had targeted nations perceived to be allies of Ukraine. Recently, it said, members of the network had tried to recruit multiple people in the United States. Authorities said the network this summer recruited an individual based in the United States to surveil and murder a prominent Russian dissident it believed to be residing in the United States. The indictment said a person identified only as “US Resident-1” had been sent to two locations associated with the targeted victim and was given “explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance” while being promised $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the work. After conducting the surveillance and providing multiple photographs and videos of locations associated with the intended victim to one of the men charged in the indictment, the US resident turned down the $40,000 that was offered to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target through murder. When the offer was rejected, the member of the intelligence services who had made it tried to recruit multiple other people within the United States to do the job by offering them substantial amounts of money, the indictment said. Photograph: Getty Images View image in fullscreen Anthony Albanese (left) challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. Photograph: Getty Images Medicare Australia AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’ Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidents Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy and Krishani Dhanji Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Technology experts have warned revelations an artificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s internal systems will not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese , challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, on Thursday after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. OpenAI alerted the government earlier this month to the June hacking via an email to a public-facing address, a situation Albanese called “obviously unacceptable”. An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so far Read more But the Australian Council on AI Strategy chief executive, Anna-Maria Arabia, said the case was unlikely to be an isolated incident. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “All of the evidence shows that our operating systems are vulnerable,” she told Guardian Australia. “Frontier AI now has capability to expose those vulnerabilities at a rate quicker than we can keep up, quicker than we can patch them. “When the companies are undertaking tests in what they think are secure environments, and when there are breaches of those environments and these incidences do happen, whether it’s accidental or not, what we’re seeing is the frontier AI capability exposing these vulnerabilities. “All evidence suggests that there is more of this to come.” Arabia said Australia needed to quickly enhance capability to detect and report incidents, and the country should host AI training labs here. Johanna Weaver, Australia’s former chief cyber negotiator at the United Nations, agreed more incidents were inevitable. Weaver is a member of the advisory board to the minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, and the executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute. “Cybersecurity experts have been warning that frontier models and AI agents could expose vulnerabilities in critical systems. What we are seeing now is the tip of the iceberg. “Governments need to draw a clear line: if companies cannot control their AI systems, they should not release them publicly.” The US Studies Centre expert Olivia Shen warned AI companies should not be allowed to decide on their own disclosure obligations for hacks and breaches. “We just don’t know how big the problem is. It could be the tip of the iceberg, but either way, we can’t be ignoring the risk. “It’s all happening at a time when Australia is designing our national standards on AI. It hasn’t been entirely clear if those national standards were going to be very hyper-focused on datacentres and leave governance questions as a bit of a bolt-on. “I think this strengthens the argument that you need to have some pretty clear standards, even just based on mandatory incident reporting, built in.” Intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is reviewing how prepared the government is to block and respond to hacking by AI. Officials will look at policies around how AI companies should report cyber-incidents to the government, and how cooperative companies should be during and after an attack. It will also investigate whether the current laws and systems are adequate to stop AI, and how government systems can be strengthened. The shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, called for Australia to develop its own domestic AI capability, instead of relying on the US. “If there’s rogue AI agents out there, we need to have our own defensive AI agents protecting Australian government data, our private sector, and other things that are important to us,” he said. The Greens demanded Labor call in the new US ambassador, David Brat, to establish what President Donald Trump knew about the attack. “This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose,” acting leader, Mehreen Faruqi, said. “The fact that the government did not even know it happened is disturbing.” Explore more on these topics Medicare Australia Anthony Albanese AI (artificial intelligence) OpenAI Hacking news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.islands.com/2281548/european.text: Destinations Europe 5 European Sauna Rules American Tourists Break Within The First 10 Minutes By Tosh Bene Oct. 12, 2026 4:45 pm EST Miljan Zivkovic/Shutterstock Add Islands on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Traveling can sometimes leave your body feeling like you've done multiple gym workouts without a day off, and let's not even get started on some of the mattresses you're expected to sleep on along the way. By the time you've spent all day trekking through a new city, your shoulders may be begging for mercy the moment you finally peel off your backpack. Luckily, there's one glorious way to soothe those travel-weary muscles: a trip to a European sauna. But before you happily steam your way to relaxation, there's one little thing to know. Just as every country has its own culture, customs, and social rules, European saunas come with their own set of unwritten etiquette, too. And if you're an American tourist, there are five rules you can very easily break within your first 10 minutes — potentially turning your blissful spa escape into an awkward cultural misstep. As a traveler, you value immersing yourself in new cultures, so you're excited to embrace the experience and give the sauna a try. But just as you approach the sauna room, the receptionist stops you in your tracks and sternly says, "No bathing suits allowed." You look concerned and suddenly find yourself sweating before you've even stepped inside. This may come as a surprise to many American travelers, but sauna etiquette varies across Europe, and clothing rules are among the most commonly misunderstood. Apart from removing your clothing and exposing your bare skin to complete strangers, other common sauna no-no's in Europe revolve around not showering before entering, talking too loudly, and bringing your phone inside. Knowing these common European sauna rules before you go could make the difference between the relaxing experience you dreamed of and one you'd rather forget. Not checking to see if full nudity is required StockLite/Shutterstock One surefire way to earn the title of "that American tourist" is to stroll into a European sauna wearing a bathing suit, only to discover that everyone else is completely, unapologetically naked. When it comes to public nudity, Western culture tends to be noticeably more modest than much of Europe. But even across Europe, sauna etiquette isn't one-size-fits-all. In Germany, for example, full nudity is considered perfectly normal — even in mixed-gender saunas. Head to Iceland, on the other hand, and you'll be expected to keep your bathing suit on , particularly in mixed-gender settings. In Finland — home to the world's sauna capital – nudity is ingrained within the sauna culture, which is so important to Finnish people that it was added to the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity . But regardless of the country, the rules and expectations will very much vary from sauna to sauna. So, how do you know when it's time to ditch the swimsuit and embrace your birthday suit? When in doubt, the safest bet is to ask someone who works at the sauna, or simply check any posted signage. In an r/AskEurope Reddit thread, one sauna enthusiast explains that embracing nudity can actually help sauna-goers blend in and take some of the awkwardness out of being bare-skinned, saying , "if everyone is [bare], that becomes the new normal, and people feel comfortable. If only some people [were], this wouldn't be the case." Speaking loudly or bringing a cell phone into the sauna Delunastudio/Getty Images Some of the best places in the world for a stress-free vacation can be found in Europe, and quiet saunas are certainly among them. Visiting a sauna isn't just about sweating away aches and pains, though — it's also a place to relax, unwind, and escape the constant pings and distractions of our cell phones, even if only for a little while. If there's one way to stand out (and not in a good way) as a tourist, it's by being too loud, or even worse, bringing your phone into a sauna. Not only does this disrupt the peace that many sauna revelers cherish, but it's also a major infringement on others' privacy (especially when nudity is involved). While conversation between others isn't necessarily frowned upon, in a European sauna it's best to read the room. If groups of friends are chatting in a low murmur, it's perfectly fine to do the same. The same goes for silence. If no one is talking, chances are you shouldn't be either. In Hungary , some sauna or spa experiences might include a short nap in designated rooms with beds, so speaking loudly — or at all — isn't encouraged. And while it might be tempting to snap a selfie as you enjoy the European sauna lifestyle, taking photos inside the sauna is generally not welcomed — especially in Nordic saunas. Not drinking enough water before getting into a sauna PeopleImages/Shutterstock If you've ever spent even 30 minutes in a sauna and noticed yourself feeling unusually sleepy or dizzy afterward, it may be more than just the effects of a relaxing sweat session. Chances are, you haven't had enough water. While traveling may cause some tourists to forget about their water intake, before and after spending time in a sauna isn't the time to disregard hydration. Sauna use can certainly leave you feeling thirsty, but failing to stay properly hydrated can become dangerous and put significant stress on your body. On average, a person can lose around half a liter to one liter (17 to 34 ounces) of fluids through sweating during just 30 minutes in a sauna. If those fluids aren't replaced, you may begin to experience dizziness, fatigue, headaches, and even fainting. This is especially important to keep in mind when alcohol is involved. Some European saunas and spas offer alcoholic drinks, and in certain places, sipping a beer while soaking is simply part of the experience. Poland and the Czech Republic , for example, are known for spas that incorporate beer into their wellness offerings. But while a beer may be part of the experience, staying hydrated is still key. The combination of heat, sweating, and alcohol can cause you to become intoxicated more quickly , while also increasing the risk of dehydration. If you choose to indulge in a beer spa, be sure to take regular sips of water as well. So, what exactly is a beer spa, and where can you find one ? In Iceland, locals and tourists alike love soaking in beer for a unique spa day . It's an unusual twist on the traditional spa experience and one that combines the relaxing effects of a warm soak with the novelty of beer. Not showering before entering the sauna Hoby Finn/Getty Images This TikTok video parodies the difference between American and European sauna cultures, showing how most Americans will walk into a sauna fully clothed, dripping in sweat, and sit down without even showering or rinsing off. While this may be normal for some Americans, doing this in Europe as a tourist can be a big no-no. Whether you're traveling to Austria or Hungary, there's one spa rule you'll want to remember: Always shower before stepping into the sauna. Throughout Europe, it's widely expected that guests shower fully unclad, clean thoroughly with soap, and rinse off completely before entering a sauna. Finnish households revere the sauna as their most sterile environment. Because these spaces routinely hosted childbirth, a strict tradition of showering beforehand emerged to preserve their exceptional hygienic standards. Even if you feel clean already, taking a quick shower helps keep the space fresh, minimizes odors, and maintains a clean, hygienic environment for everyone. Not only will your sauna mates appreciate the cleanliness, but heat can also intensify any perfumes or fragrances lingering on your body. This can create stronger scents that may be unpleasant for some, particularly those with allergies or who are sensitive to migraines. Not using a towel to sit on the sauna benches Mladen Mitrinovic/Shutterstock One of the first things to know about European sauna etiquette is what to do with your towel. In a traditional sauna, you'll often be expected to bring one with you and sit on it while using the wooden benches. This is partly for hygiene, as it keeps your body from touching the bench directly, and partly to protect the wood from sweat and natural body oils. If you're not entirely comfortable being without clothes, you can also use the towel to cover yourself. However, before you walk in with a towel in hand, it's worth checking the rules with the people who work at the sauna or spa. Sauna customs can vary depending on the type of sauna and where you are. In countries like Hungary , for instance, towels are allowed in dry saunas but should be left outside when entering a steam sauna.
